Assignment Version 
1.0 
 
The goal of the project assignments is to gain practical experience in applying several database 
management concepts and techniques using the PostgreSQL DBMS. In particular, this 
assignment mainly focuses on improving database efficiency with views, indexing and query 
planning, and on understanding what the DBMS does when transactions run concurrently. 
Your main task is to first populate your database with the supplied data, then design, implement, 
and test the appropriate queries to perform the tasks explained in the next sections. 
You must work on this project individually. Academic integrity policies apply. Please refer to 
3.60.04 Student Integrity and Misconduct of the University Policy for more information. 
This document is in three sections: This section describes the database schema for the 
assignment and provides instructions on downloading the script file needed to create and 
populate the database. The middle section describes the tasks to be completed for this 
assignment. The final section describes the submission guidelines and marking scheme. 
Enjoy the project! 
Section 1 - The FleetDB Database 
You are a developer working on FleetDB. 
Cooee Car Share is a member-owned car-sharing co-operative. Members reserve a vehicle 
online, collect it from a parking station, drive it, and return it to a station. FleetDB records the fleet, 
the membership, and every booking event. It has five tables: 
• 
STATIONS records each parking station where vehicles are picked up and dropped off; 
• 
MODELS records the specification shared by every vehicle of a given model, including its body 
type and replacement value; 
• 
VEHICLES records each individual vehicle in the fleet, its model, and its home station; 
• 
MEMBERS records each member of the co-operative. Members may be sponsored by another 
member — a business account sponsors a team account, which in turn sponsors the staff 
who drive. sponsor_id points to the sponsoring member, and is NULL for an account that 
pays its own way; 
• 
BOOKING_EVENTS is an append-only log of everything that happens to a vehicle: Reserve, 
Collect, Return, Cancel and Incident events, each stamped with the member responsible.

2 
amount holds the fare charged on a Return and the damage charge raised on an Incident; 
it is NULL for every other event type. 
 
Entity-Relationship diagram 
The tables are created as follows. 
CREATE TABLE STATIONS ( 
    station_id    VARCHAR PRIMARY KEY, 
    station_name  VARCHAR NOT NULL, 
    suburb        VARCHAR NOT NULL, 
    bays          INTEGER NOT NULL); 
  
CREATE TABLE MODELS ( 
    model_code        VARCHAR PRIMARY KEY, 
    make              VARCHAR NOT NULL, 
    model_name        VARCHAR NOT NULL, 
    body_type         VARCHAR NOT NULL, 
    seats             INTEGER NOT NULL, 
    replacement_value INTEGER NOT NULL); 
  
CREATE TABLE VEHICLES ( 
    vehicle_id    VARCHAR PRIMARY KEY, 
    model_code    VARCHAR NOT NULL REFERENCES MODELS, 
    station_id    VARCHAR NOT NULL REFERENCES STATIONS, 
    in_service    DATE NOT NULL, 
    odometer      INTEGER NOT NULL); 
  
CREATE TABLE MEMBERS ( 
    member_id     SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, 
    member_name   VARCHAR NOT NULL, 
    email         VARCHAR NOT NULL UNIQUE, 
    joined        DATE NOT NULL, 
    plan          VARCHAR NOT NULL, 
    sponsor_id    INTEGER REFERENCES MEMBERS); 
  
CREATE TABLE BOOKING_EVENTS ( 
    event_id      SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,

3 
    member_id     INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES MEMBERS, 
    vehicle_id    VARCHAR NOT NULL REFERENCES VEHICLES, 
    event_type    VARCHAR NOT NULL, 
    event_time    TIMESTAMP NOT NULL, 
    amount        NUMERIC(8,2)); 
Notes on the schema 
Two details of the schema will matter later: 
1. MEMBERS.sponsor_id is a self-referencing foreign key, and sponsorship chains can be 
more than one level deep. 
2. MEMBERS.email carries a UNIQUE constraint, so PostgreSQL has already built an index over 
it. 
Further, the trigger BI_COLLECT and its associated user-defined function UDF_BI_COLLECT have 
been added to the BOOKING_EVENTS table. This trigger treats a vehicle's most recent event as its 
current state, and refuses to record a Collect that would break the co-operative's rules:

Setup 
Before starting work on this assignment, run the setup file a2-2026-fleetdb.sql from psql with 
the \i command (it may take a minute): 
\i a2-2026-fleetdb.sql 
The script drops and recreates a database called assignment2 and leaves you connected to it, 
so your work on this assignment is kept separate from your other work. Wait until you see the 
message DONE! All data has been inserted. 
The setup file is available on Blackboard, and with mget as follows: 
mget -O /infs2200/stor/data/assignments/2/a2-2026-fleetdb.sql 
Note: as of this version of the assignment, the setup script version is 1.0

4 
 
Section 2 - Assignment 2 Tasks 
Q1 Views (4 marks total) 
Q1.1 View A (1.5 marks) 
The co-operative's planners want to know where each kind of vehicle is actually being picked up, 
so they can decide where to add parking bays. 
(1) Create a view V_BUSIEST_BAYS that reports, for each body type, the single station at which 
vehicles of that body type have been collected the most times. The view should show the body 
type, the station name, and the number of collections, ordered from most collections to fewest. (1 
mark) 
Hint: this is a "top item within each group" problem. Consider a window function such as 
RANK() or ROW_NUMBER() with a PARTITION BY clause, and use Common Table Expressions 
to build the query up in a semantically meaningful way. 
(2) Query the view (SELECT * FROM V_BUSIEST_BAYS;) and report the results. Report and 
explain the query plan. You should refer to the reported times, costs, the number of rows fetched, 
your knowledge of query planning (and anything else you feel is relevant). (0.5 marks) 
Q1.2 View B (1.5 marks) 
Every charge a member incurs is ultimately billed to the account at the top of their sponsorship 
chain. A member with no sponsor pays their own charges. A sponsored member's charges pass 
to their sponsor — and if that sponsor is itself sponsored, the charges keep passing up the chain 
until they reach an account with no sponsor. 
Create a view V_ACCOUNT_LIABILITY that identifies the ten accounts liable for the largest total 
amount charged between 1 January 2026 and 30 June 2026 inclusive. The view should show the 
account's member id, member name, and the total amount billed to it. 
Hint: the chain can be more than one level deep, so an expression such as 
COALESCE(sponsor_id, member_id) will give the wrong answer. Consider a WITH 
RECURSIVE Common Table Expression. 
Q1.3 Materialised view (1 mark) 
(1) Create a materialised view using the same query as V_ACCOUNT_LIABILITY, called 
MV_ACCOUNT_LIABILITY. (0 marks) 
(2) Report, compare and explain the following two queries, which select the contents of the view 
and the materialised view respectively. (0.5 marks) 
Query A: 
SELECT * FROM V_ACCOUNT_LIABILITY; 
Query B: 
SELECT * FROM MV_ACCOUNT_LIABILITY;

5 
You should refer to the reported times, costs, the number of rows fetched, your knowledge of 
query planning (and anything else you feel is relevant). 
(3) A member logs a large damage charge. Run the following statement, then re-run Query A and 
Query B and report what each returns. Explain the difference, then issue REFRESH MATERIALIZED 
VIEW MV_ACCOUNT_LIABILITY; and re-run Query B. In one or two sentences, state the trade-off 
a designer accepts when choosing a materialised view over an ordinary view. (0.5 marks) 
INSERT INTO BOOKING_EVENTS (member_id, vehicle_id, event_type, event_time, amount) 
SELECT member_id, 'VEH-0001', 'Incident', TIMESTAMP '2026-05-04 09:15:00', 90000.00 
FROM MEMBERS WHERE sponsor_id IS NOT NULL ORDER BY member_id DESC LIMIT 1; 
Q2 Indexes and performance (8 marks total) 
Q2.1 Composite index (3 marks) 
(1) Create an index IDX_EVENT_TYPE_TIME on the event_type and event_time fields (in that 
order) of the BOOKING_EVENTS table. (0.5 marks) 
(2) Re-run your query from Q1.1 (SELECT * FROM V_BUSIEST_BAYS;). Report the query plan. 
Compare this query plan to the one from Q1.1 and explain the differences, if any. (1.5 marks) 
(3) Now report and explain the query plan for the query below, which counts the incidents logged 
in March 2026. Explain why the planner makes different use of IDX_EVENT_TYPE_TIME here than 
it did in part (2). (1 mark) 
SELECT count(*), sum(amount) FROM BOOKING_EVENTS 
WHERE event_type = 'Incident' 
  AND event_time >= TIMESTAMP '2026-03-01' 
  AND event_time <  TIMESTAMP '2026-04-01'; 
Q2.2 Function-based index (5 marks) 
The co-operative wants to know which e-mail providers its members use, so that it can 
investigate why its newsletter is being rejected by some of them. The provider domain is the 
part of the e-mail address after the @ character. Members have entered their addresses 
inconsistently, so domains must be compared case-insensitively — Bigpond.com and 
bigpond.com are the same provider. 
(1) Write an expression that identifies each member's e-mail provider domain, and use it to report 
each distinct domain together with the number of members who use it, most popular first. You 
may use string processing functions, including the regex functions. (1 mark) 
(2) Report and explain the query plan for the query in part (1). You should refer to the reported 
times, costs, the number of rows fetched, your knowledge of query planning (and anything else 
you feel is relevant). (1 mark) 
(3) MEMBERS.email already carries a UNIQUE constraint, and therefore already has an index on it. 
In one or two sentences, explain why that existing index cannot answer a query about provider 
domains. (1 mark) 
(4) Create a function-based index called IDX_MEMBER_DOMAIN to potentially speed up queries on 
the expression from part (1). (0.5 marks) 
(5) Report the query plan, with the function-based index in place, for both of the following: 
• 
the query you wrote in part (1); and 
• 
a lookup of the members at one specific, rare provider:

6 
SELECT member_id, member_name, email FROM MEMBERS 
WHERE <your expression> = 'exemail.com.au'; 
Explain the differences to the previous plans, if any, and why the index helps one of these queries 
much more than the other. You should refer to the reported times, costs, the number of rows 
fetched, your knowledge of query planning (and anything else you feel is relevant). (1.5 marks) 
Bonus content: an index built over an expression only helps when a query contains that 
same expression. This is why production systems often store a derived value (such as a 
normalised domain) in its own column — it can then be indexed, constrained and queried 
directly. 
Q3 Query formulation and query planning (7 marks total) 
Q3.1 Two ways to ask the same question (3 marks) 
Some vehicles in the fleet have never actually been driven by a member — they may be new 
stock, or only ever reserved and then cancelled. 
(1) Write two different SQL statements that both report the vehicle_id of every vehicle that has 
never been the subject of a Collect event: (A) using NOT EXISTS; (B) without using NOT EXISTS 
or NOT IN — for example with an outer join. Both statements must return the same rows. (1.5 
marks) 
(2) Report and compare the execution plans of statements (A) and (B). Are they the same plan? 
Explain what the planner has done and why. (1.5 marks) 
Q3.2 Suppressing scan types (4 marks) 
PostgreSQL allows you to influence the query planner with runtime configuration parameters in 
psql. 
https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/runtime-config-query.html 
In this section we will suppress the use of several different scan types in order to compare 
queries. Suppressing plan types is not recommended for production, but is useful for 
understanding why one plan would be chosen over another. 
Report and explain the execution plan for the following two queries (C & D): 
3. with both index and sequential scans enabled; 
4. with index scans enabled and sequential scans suppressed; 
5. with index scans suppressed and sequential scans enabled. 
Explain why the query planner might choose one method over another. You should refer to the 
reported times and costs from the execution plan, the number of rows fetched, your knowledge of 
query planning (and anything else you feel is relevant). 
Note: For this question, bitmap and index-only scans count as index scans too. The index 
IDX_EVENT_TYPE_TIME from Q2.1 should still be in place. 
Query C: 
SELECT * FROM BOOKING_EVENTS WHERE event_type < 'Collect'; 
Query D: 
SELECT * FROM BOOKING_EVENTS WHERE event_type >= 'Collect';

7 
(2 marks for explaining up to 6 possible query plans; 2 marks for explaining the query planner's 
choices.) 
Between them, Queries C and D return every row of BOOKING_EVENTS exactly once — they differ 
only in which side of 'Collect' they take. Your explanation should account for why that is 
enough to change the plan. 
Be sure to reset index, bitmap, index-only and sequential scans back to on before proceeding to 
another question. 
Q4 Transactions (9 marks total) 
In PostgreSQL, a transaction is set up by surrounding the SQL commands of the transaction with 
BEGIN and COMMIT commands. For example, a banking transaction would look like: 
BEGIN; 
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100.00 
  WHERE name = 'Alice'; 
-- some more statements etc etc 
COMMIT; 
https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-transactions.html 
In this question we will examine what happens when two transactions occur concurrently. 
Background: how PostgreSQL reads 
You have seen two ways of keeping a concurrent schedule serialisable: locking protocols such as 
two-phase locking, and timestamp ordering. PostgreSQL uses neither of these for ordinary 
reads, so what you are about to observe will not follow from either one directly. This section gives 
you what you need; you are not expected to have met it before. 
Instead of taking read locks, a PostgreSQL query reads from a snapshot — a consistent picture 
of the database containing exactly those changes that were committed before the snapshot was 
taken. Because reading acquires no locks, readers never block writers and writers never block 
readers. 
At PostgreSQL's default isolation level, READ COMMITTED, a new snapshot is taken at the start 
of every statement. Two statements in the same transaction may therefore see different data, if 
another transaction committed in between them. 
Two consequences are worth holding on to as you work through this question: 
• 
A trigger runs inside the transaction that fired it. Any query the trigger makes is answered 
from that transaction's current snapshot. It gets no special or privileged view of the database. 
• 
A snapshot is not a lock. Reading a row records nothing and reserves nothing; it does not 
prevent another transaction from changing what you just read. 
Q4.1 A race for the same car (6 marks) 
Two members go after the same car at the same moment: 
• 
Session 1 is a member at the parking bay about to drive away. It checks that the vehicle is 
available, and then records a Collect. 
• 
Session 2 is a member on the website. It checks that the same vehicle is available, and then 
records a Reserve for three days' time, and commits — all while session 1 is still open. 
You will need two psql connections open side by side, both at the default isolation level. You can 
use the now() function to provide a timestamp. Include screenshots of both connections.

8 
(1) In your first psql connection, begin a transaction and then perform a query to identify a 
vehicle which is currently available — that is, a vehicle whose most recent event is a Return. 
Do not commit yet. (2 marks) 
(2) In your second connection, begin another transaction. Run the same availability check for the 
vehicle session 1 picked, then record a Reserve on it for some other member, 3 days in the 
future, and commit. (0.5 marks) 
(3) Back in your first connection, attempt to record a Collect on that vehicle for a different 
member at the present time, then commit. Report what happened at each step, and which event 
or events ended up recorded against the vehicle. (1 mark) 
(4) Explain the outcome, both in database terms and in car-share terms. You may include a 
schedule or precedence graph of the transaction events if it aids your explanation. (2.5 marks) 
Hint: was the answer to the query in step (1) still true by the time step (3) ran? Which 
snapshot did the BI_COLLECT trigger use when it ran? And what, if anything, stopped session 
2 from changing the answer underneath session 1? 
Q4.2 Deadlock (3 marks) 
In Q4.1 neither transaction could make progress on the other's terms, but only one of them was 
ever blocked. A deadlock is the symmetric case: two transactions each hold something the other 
is waiting for, so neither can move. Neither has done anything wrong on its own — it is the 
interleaving that traps them. 
Two staff are correcting odometer readings after a service run, and they work through the same 
two vehicles in opposite orders. 
(1) In two psql connections, begin a transaction in each. In your first connection, update the 
odometer of VEH-0401, and then the odometer of VEH-0501. In your second connection, update 
those same two vehicles in the opposite order. Run the statements one at a time so you can see 
which one blocks. Report what happened at each step, quoting any error message in full. (1.5 
marks) 
(2) Draw the wait-for graph as it stood immediately before the DBMS intervened, and mark the 
cycle on it. State what the DBMS did about the deadlock, and what became of each of the two 
transactions. (1 mark) 
(3) Name one strategy that would have prevented this deadlock rather than detecting it after the 
fact, and say what that strategy would cost the co-operative. (0.5 marks) 
Hint: an UPDATE takes a lock on the row it changes and holds it until the transaction ends. 
Which statement in each session was still waiting when the error appeared?

You will be marked primarily on the contents of your report file. However, the teaching team must 
be able to reproduce the screenshots in your report by loading a2-2026-fleetdb.sql into a

If code is not provided for any question such that your screenshots cannot be reproduced,

• 
Answers to all the questions in the Assignment Tasks section. 
• 
If you are asked to write SQL statements, you need to include those statements in your 
report. 
• 
After you execute a SQL statement, if PostgreSQL produces any output (e.g. query result, 
query execution time, query plan, etc), you should also include a screenshot of the output as 
well. 
• 
Where one sub-question asks you to write a query and a later sub-question asks you to 
report on its timing, please simply refer back to the initial screenshot. 
The presentation mark is given as follows: 
• 
Ordinary query results (not plans) do not exceed a page — any query returning more than 20 
rows may show just the first 10 and the last 10 rows. You may find some helpful instructions 
for formatting query output in Practical 1. (1 mark) 
• 
No result tuples are broken across lines, and all query plans are shown in full (if a plan takes 
more than one page, break it at an appropriate spot). (1 mark)

Q1.3 part 1 materialized view definition 
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW MV_ACCOUNT_LIABILITY AS 
WITH RECURSIVE account_tree AS ( 
    SELECT member_id, member_id AS account_id 
    FROM MEMBERS 
    WHERE sponsor_id IS NULL 
 
    UNION ALL 
 
    SELECT child.member_id, parent.account_id 
    FROM MEMBERS child 
    JOIN account_tree parent 
        ON child.sponsor_id = parent.member_id 
) 
SELECT 
    root.member_id, 
    root.member_name, 
    SUM(e.amount) AS total_amount 
FROM account_tree t 
JOIN MEMBERS root 
    ON root.member_id = t.account_id 
JOIN BOOKING_EVENTS e 
    ON e.member_id = t.member_id 
WHERE e.event_type IN ('Return', 'Incident') 
  AND e.event_time >= TIMESTAMP '2026-01-01' 
  AND e.event_time < TIMESTAMP '2026-07-01' 
GROUP BY root.member_id, root.member_name 
ORDER BY total_amount DESC, root.member_id 
LIMIT 10;

Queries C and D partition 196,441 events at this stage. C returns 8,158 rows (4.15 
percent), while D returns 188,283 (95.85 percent). The opposite inequalities on the 
same indexed column therefore have very different selectivity. 
C1 uses Bitmap Index Scan on IDX_EVENT_TYPE_TIME followed by Bitmap Heap Scan. 
Its cost is 196. 97..1937.08, with 8,329 rows estimated and 8,158 returned. Planning 
takes 4.423 ms and execution 12.443 ms. It visits 1,625 exact heap blocks; total buffers 
are 1,628 shared hits and 31 reads. Selective index access costs less than scanning and 
filtering the whole event log, even though the matching events are spread across many 
heap pages. 
D1 uses Seq Scan, with cost 0. 00..4091.51, 188,112 estimated rows and 188,283 
actual rows. Planning takes 0.937 ms and execution 24.116 ms. It reads the heap 
through 1,636 shared buffer hits and removes 8,158 nonmatching rows. Returning 
almost the whole table makes a sequential pass cheaper in the cost model than 
traversing many index entries and then visiting almost every heap page. 
C2 retains the bitmap plan and the same cost and row estimates when sequential 
scans are suppressed. Planning takes 0.103 ms and execution 2.095 ms. All 1,659 
buffer accesses are hits, including 34 for the index. The change from C1 includes a 
warmer cache; suppressing a scan type did not change the chosen access method, so 
the faster time cannot be attributed to a new plan. 
D2 uses Bitmap Index Scan plus Bitmap Heap Scan because sequential scans are 
suppressed. Its cost rises to 4370. 29..8357.69. It still returns 188,283 rows versus 
188,112 estimated and visits all 1,636 heap blocks, with 1,868 shared hits and 493 
reads overall. Planning takes 0.099 ms and execution 22.959 ms. This is slightly faster 
than D1 in this single run despite the higher estimated cost. It does not establish that 
bitmap access is generally better for this broad predicate; cache state and 
measurement variation affect elapsed time.

The schedule is T1 BEGIN and availability read; T2 BEGIN and availability read; T2 
Reserve and COMMIT; T1 Collect attempt; trigger exception; T1 ROLLBACK. T1 initially 
sees an available car, but that answer becomes stale before its next operation. 
At READ COMMITTED, each statement uses a fresh snapshot. The Collect attempt runs 
after T2 has committed, so the trigger can see the committed Reserve. The trigger 
orders events by event time and treats that future-dated reservation as the latest state. 
Because it belongs to member 2, it refuses a Collect by member 1. 
An ordinary SELECT reads without a row lock that reserves this car. Its ACCESS SHARE 
relation lock is compatible with the other transaction's insertion, so it does not prevent 
T2 from changing the answer. T1 stays open but does not retain its first statement's 
snapshot for later statements. In this schedule the rejection is a business-rule 
exception, with no circular lock wait. 
For the co-operative, the person at the parking bay is refused the car even though the 
other person reserved it three days ahead. The simplified trigger makes a future 
reservation an immediate hold. Coordinating availability checks and writes would 
address races, while interval-aware booking rules would also be needed to distinguish 
available now from reserved later.

Deadlock explanation 
T1 updates VEH-0401 by 10 and holds its row lock. T2 updates VEH-0501 by 20 and holds 
the other row lock. T1 then requests VEH-0501 and waits. While it is waiting, T2 requests 
VEH-0401, completing the cycle. Both updates cannot finish until the other transaction ends. 
PostgreSQL detects the deadlock and aborts T2 in this recorded run. T2's earlier +20 on 
VEH-0501 is undone and its locks are released. T1's waiting update resumes, returning 
122160, and T1 commits. T2's attempted COMMIT reports ROLLBACK. Final values are 
VEH-0401 = 149110 and VEH-0501 = 122160.

The full original error is shown below and transcribed without translating its diagnostic text. 
T1's reported 116906.993 ms includes the time spent waiting while the next command was 
entered in the other window. T2's error took 1019.158 ms. These are not ordinary update 
processing times. 
The wait-for graph immediately before detection has T1 -> T2 for VEH-0501 and T2 -> T1 for 
VEH-0401. Its cycle T1 -> T2 -> T1 explains why neither could proceed. The photographed 
hand drawing marks both held resources and both waiting edges. 
A consistent ascending vehicle_id lock order would prevent this cycle: every correction 
transaction must acquire VEH-0401 before VEH-0501. A transaction blocked on the first row 
would then hold no later row needed by its predecessor. The co-operative would pay with 
more waiting or queuing when corrections overlap, while unrelated vehicles could still be 
processed concurrently. The victim can differ on a rerun, so the outcome here is based on 
the actual screenshot.
